blocks.heading: Market Demand and Skill Match Come First

items.text: Market demand / future-proofing
A career can look exciting, well-paid, and secure everywhere online and still have almost no real market for your specific combination of skill and location.
Being able to admire a role and being able to become genuinely good at its daily work are two different tests.

blocks.heading: Some Factors Carry More Weight Than Others

items.text: The tier order above is not arbitrary.

Hygiene factors like pay, job security, and working conditions can create real dissatisfaction when they are missing, but adding more of them stops improving satisfaction fast once a baseline is covered.
This is the research reason pay sits in The Shape tier instead of at the very top.

blocks.heading: Shape: Pay, Growth Ceiling, and Stability Decide
blocks.sourceSectionTitle: The Shape: pay, growth ceiling, and stability decide how big this gets

rows: Look at the realistic range for someone starting out, not the outlier number in a viral post. Then separately check the ceiling - what a strong performer five or ten years in is actually earning, and whether that number comes from a fixed pay band or from something closer to ownership, specialisation, or consulting advantage.

Some roles are structurally capped: fixed pay bands, a small market, no path to lead or own anything. Others have real headroom through specialisation, a consulting or freelance track, a product or content layer, or a move into leadership. Name the specific moves that separate a median outcome from a strong one in this field - a generic "keep upskilling" line is not an answer to this factor.

Stability is not the same as government-job or big-company stability specifically - it is how exposed the role is to layoffs, automation, policy change, or seasonal demand right now, in this market, not five years ago. A role can look stable and still be exposed to a slow, quiet decline that only shows up in hiring data, not in headlines.

blocks.heading: 4 Trade-Offs No Slogan Actually Resolves
blocks.sourceSectionTitle: The 4 trade-offs no slogan actually resolves

rows: A high-interest field with weak market pay, and a well-paid field that bores you, are both common, real situations - not a failure of imagination.

Look for the overlap zone: a market-viable lane that touches your genuine interest, even at one remove, rather than the exact daydream job. A finance analyst who is genuinely curious about the businesses they analyse usually beats someone chasing the highest-interest field with no market for it.
Stable, structured-pay roles trade a lower ceiling for lower exposure to sudden change; high-growth roles trade real upside for real volatility.

Match this to your actual financial runway and life stage, not to which one sounds more impressive. Someone with dependents and no savings buffer usually needs more stability weight right now than someone testing options early with a support system behind them.
The highest-ceiling roles - specialist tracks, consulting, ownership, senior leadership - usually demand more hours and less predictability, at least early on.
Decide by life stage, not by guilt. Trading balance for ceiling for a defined stretch, with a plan to pull back later, is different from doing it indefinitely without ever naming the trade.
Families are often optimising for a version of safety that made sense for their generation's job market, not necessarily today's.
Negotiate with a plan, not a debate - target role, real cost, real demand data, and a small proof project usually move a worried parent further than an argument about feelings.

visuals.heading: These 8 Factors for Your Own Decision

items.text: Whether you can tolerate the boring, repetitive part of the work - the 80% that never shows up in the daydream version.
Whether the field has any real room to grow, or caps out at a fixed ceiling within a few years.
The unglamorous 80% of the work - the paperwork, the repetition, the waiting - that never appears in the highlight-reel version.
Whether the role fits how you personally recharge: deep solo focus, constant people contact, or a mix.
List your shortlisted options side by side.
Score each of the 8 factors 1 to 5 for how much it matters to you right now.
Score each option 1 to 5 on each factor, using real evidence.
Multiply your importance score by each option's factor score, then add the totals.
Re-run it after any real test.
